chapter_theme: Children are the greatest thing one can obtain: first for the fruit they bring beyond this life, then for sensuous joy in them, and finally for their worth in the world. It moves from possessing them to being known by them, and the last verse has the father judged by the son.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the excellence of having sons (61), the next-world fruit (62-63), the joys in this life (64-66), the father's duty (67), others' delight (68), the mother's joy (69), and the son's duty (70). Verses 67 and 70 frame the final group as a pair of debts.

61.reading: Of all that can be gained, we know of nothing else like children who come to know what should be known.
61.nuance: The first-person யாம் அறிவது is unusual and it sounds personal. The word அறிவறிந்த makes this a conditional praise: not children as such, but children who come to understand.

positions.position: The epithet of understanding restricts மக்கள் to sons, excluding daughters.
The verse is about intelligent children in general, with no such exclusion.

62.reading: Evils will not touch one for seven births, if one has children of good character who bring no blame.
62.nuance: The verse assumes a child's character can protect a parent across births. Kalaignar's reading turns seven births into seven generations, which reverses the direction from the parent's future to the descendants', but no aligned Parimelazhagar or Manakkudavar comment is available to set against it here.

63.reading: People call their children their wealth, because the wealth of those children comes by way of their own deeds.
63.nuance: தம்தம் வினை is the crux: whose deeds, and whose wealth? Pope's couplet and his own gloss take opposite sides of this.

positions.position: Sons' good deeds done on the parents' behalf bring what they earned to the parents in the next world.
positions.quote: அப்புதல்வர் செய்த பொருள் தம்மை நோக்கி அவர் செய்யும் நல்வினையானே தம்பால் வரும்

positions.position: Each child's wealth comes from that child's own actions.
positions.quote: அம்மக்களின் பொருள்கள் அவரவர் செயல்களின் விளைவாக வரக் கூடியவை.

64.reading: Far sweeter than amrita is the plain gruel stirred by the small hands of one's own children.
64.nuance: The food is கூழ், a humble gruel, and it is sweet because of the mess. Parimelazhagar illustrates the mess by citing Purananuru 188, which makes this verse a real thread across books.

65.reading: Touching one's children is joy to the body, and hearing their words is joy to the ear.
65.nuance: The chapter dwells on the senses here, after verses that praise restraining them. Parimelazhagar notes that சொல் is deliberately general, so it covers grown learned speech as well as baby talk.

66.reading: 'The flute is sweet, the lute is sweet', say those who haven't heard their own children's prattle.
66.nuance: The verse never actually says prattle is sweeter. It leaves that to be inferred, and Parimelazhagar notes this implied ending. Such praise comes in the form of mild scorn for the musically refined.

67.reading: The good a father does for a son is to make him sit at the front in the assembly.
67.nuance: Parimelazhagar rules out nepotism: the son must actually surpass the assembly in learning. He adds that making him rich is no real good, since wealth brings pain.

68.reading: Their children's understanding is sweet to all beings on the great earth, more than to themselves.
68.nuance: தம்மின், than themselves, can attach to two different things. Pope's couplet and gloss again split, one on each side.

positions.position: It is sweeter to all the world, especially the assembly, than it is to the parents.
It concerns children who are wiser than their parents, which gladdens everyone.
positions.quote: பெற்றோரைக் காட்டிலும் பிள்ளைகள் அறிவிற் சிறந்து விளங்கினால்,

69.reading: A mother who hears her son called worthy rejoices more than at the hour she bore him.
69.nuance: The verse says she hears. Parimelazhagar's explanation is his own and is telling: he says women cannot know this for themselves. The verse may simply show that public recognition is what is wanted. It sets the birth's joy as the baseline and goes beyond it.

positions.position: She has to hear it because, by a woman's nature, she cannot judge it herself.

70.reading: The help a son gives his father is the saying, 'What penance did this one's father do?'
70.nuance: The repayment is a sentence spoken by others. The son can't deliver it directly, only live so that others say it. The verse uses the language of austerity (நோற்றான்), so fatherhood is framed as a kind of penance.

links.note: Rain is the world's amrita in 11, and in 64 a child's messy gruel beats amrita. The same word is the top of two different scales: what sustains all life, and what is sweet to one parent.

Parimelazhagar's two comments pull apart. On 63 a son's good deeds reach his parents. On 377 he says the fruit of one soul's deed never goes to another (ch038). The verses themselves don't settle how merit is shared.

The father's debt and the son's debt form an exchange: he gives the learning that seats the son at the front, and the son gives back a sentence of praise. Parimelazhagar's gloss on 70 makes the link explicit by calling the father 'the one who made him learned'.

source_issues: Parimelazhagar's entry for verse 62 is a duplicate of his comment on verse 61, so it is misaligned and hasn't been used. His note at 63 does say that verses 62-63 concern the next-world fruit.
Parimelazhagar's entry for verse 66 begins at the விளக்கம், without the word-by-word gloss. His entry for verse 69 starts with a stray '>'.
Manakkudavar is not aligned for verses 62, 67 and 70. His entry for verse 66 ends with a stray '6'.
Kalaignar's entry for verse 64 ends with a stray '65.'.
